title: Right Frame, Wrong Rule: Cultural Cues Expose the Financial Knowledge Gap They Were Meant to Close
abstract: When a question has valid answers under different normative frameworks, a language model must decide which framework to use and whether it can answer correctly within it. We call this setting normative pluralism and study it in Islamic finance using a four-choice taxonomy that separates framework selection from within-framework correctness. This separation reveals the stereotype trap: a cultural cue steers a model toward one framework, but the model selects an incorrect answer within that framework. Across twelve models, two languages, and fifty demographic signals, cultural cues change framework selection and reveal substantial differences in accuracy, especially among non-frontier models. Under the strongest signal, large open-weight models select the Islamic framework 97% of the time. A two-choice evaluation would report near-perfect alignment, although 57--66% of those selections are incorrect. These findings motivate, but do not directly test, the competence-conditioned routing hypothesis: models may favor frameworks where they are more accurate, while cultural cues may expose framework-specific competence gaps.

title: Non-Prehensile Throwing: A Reinforcement Learning Perspective
abstract: Robotic throwing enables fast object transport and extends a robot's reachable workspace beyond traditional pick-and-place. While prehensile (grasp-based) throwing works well for graspable items, non-prehensile (grasp-free) throwing is better suited for large, heavy, and/or deformable objects. Existing approaches rely on model-based optimization with simplified contact models (e.g., dynamic grasping) and low-dimensional trajectory parameterizations, which limit solution quality and reachable workspace. We propose a reinforcement learning approach that additionally leverages sliding and rolling contact modes and directly optimizes joint-space trajectories without analytical contact models or custom parameterizations. The Markov Decision Process (MDP) is formulated as a dynamical system that evolves the robot's joint state conditioned on the throwing target, object model, and initial configuration. Joint-jerk trajectories are planned offline at a low control rate and upsampled into smooth, high-rate velocity commands for deployment. For sim-to-real transfer, we minimize the robot-dynamics gap through minimum-jerk system identification and train uncertainty-aware policies to mitigate object-modeling errors, particularly sensitivity to dynamic friction. In simulation, the policy achieves 99% success across thousands of configurations and generalizes to unseen objects. Sensitivity analysis shows robustness to mass uncertainty but high sensitivity to dynamic friction, consistent with the sliding-based release mechanism. Deployed zero-shot on a UR5e operating near its physical limits (5 m/s end-effector velocity), our method throws diverse objects including heavy (790 g) and large (20x20x28 cm) items to targets up to 350 cm distance or 180 cm elevation, achieving a 97% real-world success rate.

title: Same Semantics, Different Outcome: On the Modality Robustness of Multimodal LLMs under Knowledge Conflict
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly provided with contextual evidence in heterogeneous forms: as a text passage, as a rendered image of the same passage, or as both together. However, it remains unclear how consistently these surface forms are processed, especially when the evidence conflicts with the model's parametric knowledge. We study modality robustness under knowledge conflict across 13 MLLMs and two datasets, and find them far from robust. (1) Contrary to common belief, models favor a context that contradicts parametric knowledge more readily in image form than in text form; (2) when a contradicting text and image are presented together, the preferred modality is essentially arbitrary, varying with input order, model, and dataset. We further demonstrate that this instability has practical consequences: it degrades performance in multimodal RAG and can be exploited by adversarial attacks. To alleviate this brittleness, we examine several simple techniques---prompting, steering, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and direct preference optimization; the majority prove ineffective, whereas SFT achieves moderate success. We therefore call for greater awareness of this inconsistency and argue that it is fundamental, demanding attention at multiple training stages.

title: Multi-Scale Lung Nodule Detection in CT Images Using YOLOv8-ACPA With Machine Learning-Based False Positive Reduction
abstract: Lung cancer has been reported to account for approximately 1.8 million deaths annually and remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Early detection of pulmonary nodules using low-dose CT imaging is considered critical; however, manual interpretation has been shown to exhibit high inter-observer variability. In this study, a novel detection framework, YOLOv8-ACPA, has been proposed by integrating an Adaptive Context Pyramid Attention (ACPA) module as a parameter-efficient, drop-in replacement for CBAM across all five backbone stages of YOLOv8. The ACPA module has been designed to enhance feature representation through three complementary mechanisms: (1) multi-scale contextual extraction using parallel depthwise dilated convolutions with dilation rates of {1, 3, 6}; (2) an uncertainty-aware gate (UAG) that estimates per-channel local variance and suppresses vessel-like noise patterns; and (3) pyramid channel recalibration (PCR) that generates adaptive attention weights from multi-scale feature descriptors. Furthermore, the proposed pipeline has been extended with a 57-dimensional radiomics-based XGBoost classifier to reduce false-positive detections. Experimental evaluation on LIDC-IDRI slices has demonstrated a CPM of 0.931 ± 0.008(95% CI: [0.921, 0.941]), sensitivity of 95.7 ± 1.2% at 4 FP/scan (95% CI: [94.2%, 97.2%]), and an AUC-ROC of 0.964 ± 0.006(95% CI: [0.957, 0.971]); intervals computed via a t-distribution (df = 4) over the five independent runs. After false-positive reduction, the system achieved 1.4 FP/scan, indicating consistent improvement over the baseline YOLOv8 model (p < 0.001). A full layer-by-layer PyTorch implementation with detailed tensor shapes and parameter counts has been provided to ensure reproducibility.

title: THE EVOLUTION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TO GENERATIVE AI: FROM SYMBOLIC REASONING TO CREATIVE MACHINES
abstract: Artificial intelligence has developed in a number of steps. These series of steps include symbolic, decision-based systems, statistical machine learning methods, deep learning, and the large-scale, multi-modal generative systems. This chapter focuses on the emergence of generative AI (GenAI) such as large language models, image, video diffusion systems, and agentic architecture. Relying on recent surveys and domain-specific literature, the chapter examines the key architectural innovations that enabled the shift from logical problem-solving to generative modeling. It focuses on the use of generative AI across education, finance, healthcare, ecology, advertising, and scholarly publishing. It further considers the ethical, governance, and societal questions that have accompanied this diffusion, and closes by examining agentic AI as the next evolutionary step, in which generative models are coupled with planning and autonomous tool use. The chapter talks about the evolution of AI, which is not only a single technological leap but a layered, cumulative process. The chapter argues that the evolution of generative AI is best understood not as a single technological leap but as a layered, cumulative process in which algorithmic innovation, infrastructural scaling, domain adoption, and governance responses have made advancements.

title: Celebes Shrew Rat: A Novel Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by the Behavior of *Tupaia minor*
abstract: This paper presents Celebes Shrew Rat (CSR), a new metaheuristic algorithm designed to address complex optimization problems. The algorithm is inspired by the foraging behavior of *Tupaia minor*, the Celebes shrew rat, a small, nocturnal mammal known for its efficient and adaptive searching strategies. CSR leverages the animal's exploratory and exploitative behaviors – characterized by rapid, short-range movements followed by deliberate, longer-range jumps – to navigate the search space. The algorithm utilizes a novel representation of the solution space, a "rat's nest" structure, and a dynamically adjusted jump length and stride frequency based on the local search landscape. Performance evaluations are presented on a range of benchmark functions, demonstrating CSR's competitive capabilities alongside established metaheuristic methods. The key contributions of this work lie in the novel rat's nest representation, the adaptive jump control mechanism, and the overall inspired design that mimics the observed foraging behavior of *Tupaia minor*. The algorithm's efficiency and adaptability are showcased, suggesting its potential for applications in diverse optimization domains.

title: Dynamic Probability Field Theory: Adaptive Information Volume Calculation
abstract: This paper explores the application of dynamic probability field theory to the precise calculation of probability distributions within complex systems. Traditional probabilistic models often struggle with uncertainty, requiring approximations that can compromise accuracy. We propose a novel approach that dynamically adjusts the probability field's complexity based on environmental uncertainty, allowing for more accurate and robust predictions. This work centers on a self-adaptive calculation algorithm for complex systems, leveraging the inherent computational demands of dynamic probability field theory. The core mechanism involves a refined approach to information volume estimation, addressing the limitations of static models in dealing with evolving uncertainty. This development offers a significant advancement in the modeling and prediction of systems characterized by dynamic change.

title: Formal Model of Collective Intelligence in Distributed Computing Systems
abstract: This paper presents a formal mathematical model for collective intelligence (CI) within distributed computing systems. The core claim is that a rigorous mathematical framework can accurately represent the emergent behavior often observed in CI systems. This model utilizes a stochastic process approach, blending aspects of agent-based modeling and network theory, to simulate the dynamic interactions between computational agents. Specifically, we define a system of interacting agents, each with a specific set of attributes and behaviors, operating within a network structure. The model incorporates stochastic elements to account for the inherent uncertainty in agent interactions and network dynamics. The key output of this model is the prediction of emergent collective behaviors, quantified using measures such as consensus, diversity, and innovation. We demonstrate the model's ability to capture key CI phenomena, providing a theoretical foundation for understanding and designing CI systems. The model's development focuses on a clear mathematical representation, allowing for both quantitative analysis and further theoretical extensions.

title: ## Bulldog Rat: A Novel Metaheuristic Optimization Algorithm Inspired by Bulldog Rat Behavior
abstract: This paper proposes a novel metaheuristic optimization algorithm, Bulldog Rat, inspired by the foraging behavior of bulldog rats. These rats exhibit a unique strategy of repeatedly searching a defined area, alternating between two distinct search modes: a rapid, short-range exploration and a slower, long-range scanning. Bulldog Rat leverages this behavior to create a robust and efficient optimization algorithm. The algorithm utilizes a population of candidate solutions, employing a dynamic switching mechanism between exploration and exploitation phases, mimicking the bulldog rat's alternating search patterns. The core components include a population initialization, a dynamic switching parameter controlling the balance between exploration and exploitation, and a convergence criterion based on population diversity. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on a suite of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its competitive capability compared to established metaheuristic algorithms such as Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Genetic Algorithm (GA). The results highlight the effectiveness of the bulldog rat-inspired approach and suggest potential applications in various complex optimization tasks.

title: Dynamic Programming with Quantum-Inspired Search Algorithms
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of accelerating dynamic programming (DP) algorithms by incorporating search strategies derived from quantum mechanics, specifically quantum tunneling and superposition. The core premise is that the inherent exploration capabilities of quantum phenomena can be simulated through quantum-inspired search algorithms, such as quantum annealing or evolutionary algorithms mimicking tunneling behavior, to efficiently navigate the solution space of DP problems. We propose a framework where a classical DP algorithm is augmented with a quantum-inspired search component. The aim is to leverage the strengths of both approaches – the precision and systematic nature of DP combined with the potentially faster exploration offered by quantum-inspired techniques. The effectiveness of this approach is evaluated through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, focusing on scenarios where traditional DP methods struggle with large state spaces or complex decision boundaries. This research contributes to a new paradigm in algorithm design, bridging the gap between classical and quantum computing by utilizing quantum-inspired methods to optimize classical algorithms. The core idea is to treat the DP problem as a tunneling event within a high-dimensional space, significantly reducing the time required to find optimal solutions.

title: Brown Bear: A Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by Brown Bear Behavior
abstract: This paper presents Brown Bear, a novel metaheuristic algorithm designed to address complex optimization problems. The algorithm is inspired by the foraging behavior of brown bears, specifically their strategies for finding and securing food resources. Brown Bear utilizes a combination of exploration and exploitation phases, mimicking the bear's scouting and focused searching patterns. The core of the algorithm involves a dynamic agent population, where each agent represents a potential solution. These agents move through the search space, guided by a distance-based movement strategy that reflects the bear's tendency to move towards areas with higher food density. The algorithm incorporates a novel 'comfort zone' mechanism, modeled after a bear's preference for established feeding grounds, to prevent premature convergence. The performance of Brown Bear is evaluated on a range of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness and adaptability. The algorithm's key features include: a dynamically adjusted population size, a distance-based movement mechanism, a 'comfort zone' constraint, and a probabilistic selection strategy. Results indicate that Brown Bear offers competitive performance compared to established metaheuristic algorithms such as the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and the Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) algorithm. Further research will explore the algorithm's potential in various application domains.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic probability field theory that allows for automatic parameter adjustment of probability distributions during computation. We explore the core mechanism of this adaptation, demonstrating its effectiveness through a series of simulations and analysis. The resulting system exhibits enhanced responsiveness and adaptability, representing a significant advancement in computational modeling.

title: 基于图的量子状态的统计学分析
abstract: This paper presents a novel statistical analysis method based on graph representation for quantum states, aiming to provide theoretical guidance for quantum computing optimization. The core idea is to leverage the inherent structure of quantum states represented as graphs to derive statistical properties and identify optimal parameters for quantum algorithms. The method employs graph-based density estimation and quantum state propagation to analyze and predict the behavior of quantum systems, offering a more efficient and insightful approach than traditional methods. The paper details the implementation of the algorithm, discusses its performance characteristics, and explores its potential impact on quantum algorithm design and optimization. We highlight the advantages of this approach, focusing on its ability to capture complex correlations within quantum states and provide quantitative insights into system properties.

title: Bornean Ferret Badger: A Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by the Foraging Behavior of *Melogale moschata*
abstract: This paper presents Bornean Ferret Badger (BFB), a novel metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the foraging strategies of *Melogale moschata*, a small, nocturnal mammal found in Borneo. The algorithm leverages the animal's efficient path planning, selective resource exploitation, and adaptive adjustment of search parameters—characteristics observed in its natural behavior—to develop a robust optimization technique. BFB combines elements of Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Simulated Annealing (SA) with a unique 'Foraging Intensity' parameter that dynamically adjusts the exploration-exploitation balance. The algorithm's performance is evaluated across a range of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions with reasonable computational cost. The core innovation lies in the adaptive modulation of the search space based on an emulation of the badger's ability to prioritize high-value resource locations. The algorithm's key parameters – population size (N), inertia weight (w), cognitive coefficient (c1), social coefficient (c2), temperature (T), cooling rate (α), and foraging intensity (FI) – are discussed in detail, along with their influence on the algorithm's convergence and solution quality. The results show that BFB can be a competitive alternative to existing metaheuristic methods, particularly in problems exhibiting complex landscapes and the need for balanced exploration and exploitation.

title: Distributed Memoryless Kernel Learning
abstract: Kernel learning provides a powerful framework for non-linear classification and regression by implicitly mapping data into a high-dimensional feature space. However, traditional kernel learning methods often suffer from significant computational and memory limitations, particularly when dealing with large datasets. This paper proposes a novel distributed algorithm for learning kernel functions that addresses these challenges. The algorithm leverages a memoryless kernel representation and locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) to enable efficient iterative training across multiple nodes. The core idea is to avoid storing the entire kernel matrix, drastically reducing memory consumption. Our approach utilizes a distributed architecture where each node maintains a local view of the data and iteratively updates a shared kernel representation based on LSH-indexed updates. We demonstrate that this distributed approach significantly reduces the computational and memory burden associated with kernel learning, enabling the training of larger kernels compared to traditional methods. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through theoretical analysis and, importantly, through detailed mathematical derivations that justify the efficiency gains. We present a rigorous framework for understanding the convergence properties of the distributed learning process. The key contributions of this work are the memoryless kernel representation and the LSH-based distributed update strategy, offering a scalable solution for kernel learning problems.

title: Probabilistic Programming with Latent Variable Discovery via Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Probabilistic programming languages offer a flexible framework for modeling complex systems with uncertainty. However, a significant challenge lies in the discovery and interpretation of latent variables – hidden factors that drive the observed data. Traditional probabilistic programming approaches often rely on hand-crafted assumptions about these latent variables, which can be both time-consuming and prone to error. This work introduces a novel approach that integrates a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) directly into the probabilistic programming workflow. The GAN learns a compact and informative latent representation of the data, effectively uncovering latent variables without explicit specification. The probabilistic program then leverages this learned representation to perform inference, prediction, and ultimately, a more intuitive understanding of the underlying system. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this hybrid approach through a series of examples, showcasing its ability to handle complex models and improve the accuracy and interpretability of probabilistic inference. The core innovation rests on the automated latent variable discovery facilitated by the GAN, offering a significant advancement over conventional probabilistic programming techniques.

title: Training Without Gathering the Data: A Historical Development Review of Federated Learning and Privacy-Preserving AI
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Federated Learning and Privacy-Preserving AI in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of federated learning and privacy as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: Improved MADDPG Algorithm for Cooperative Pursuit via Joint Optimization of Experience Quality and Efficiency
authors: ZHANG Hongqiang, HU Kai, WU Lianghong, WANG Xi, ZUO Cili, CHEN Lei, LIU Chaohua, CHEN Zuguo
abstract: To address training oscillations and slow policy convergence caused by poor experience quality and low utilization efficiency in multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MARL) for cooperative pursuit tasks, an improved algorithm, STEP-MADDPG (sequence-temporal experience prioritized multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient) is proposed to synergistically optimize experience quality and efficiency. It constructs a dual-layer optimization framework featuring a “sample denoising and sequence guidance” closed-loop mechanism for the synergistic optimization of experience quality and efficiency. In the experience quality enhancement layer, long short-term memory (LSTM) networks extract temporal dependencies from observation sequences in partially observable environments, while the input structure of value network (Critic) is reconstructed to align the hidden states of policy network (Actor). Furthermore, a ternary decoupled sampling (TDS) strategy mitigates sample distribution conflicts between the Actor and Critic. By integrating the loss-adjusted prioritized mechanism (LAP) with inverse prioritized sampling, TDS filters high-confidence experiences for the Actor, reducing gradient variance and enhancing training stability. In the experience efficiency optimization layer, prioritized sequence experience replay (PSER) focuses the model on critical experience sequences. Concurrently, an adaptive mixed sampling mechanism dynamically adjusts sample weights for exploration and exploitation during policy updates. The distribution correction effect of this mechanism inversely stabilizes the input distribution of quality layer, reducing temporal feature extraction uncertainty. Simulations conducted in 2D pursuit scenarios involving static and dynamic targets and obstacles demonstrate that the proposed STEP-MADDPG algorithm significantly outperforms baseline algorithms in terms of convergence speed and pursuit success rate across all evaluated scenarios. In fully dynamic scenarios, convergence speed improves by 29% to 42%, and the pursuit success rate increases by 6% to 25%.

abstract: Artificial Intelligence is changing business-customer connections. This paper explains AI-driven marketing. AI tools help understand customers. They create more relevant marketing campaigns. Businesses study customer data. They group customers effectively. They recommend products intelligently. Chatbots answer questions instantly. AI predicts buying behaviour. It also generates marketing content. These capabilities save significant time. Customer experience improves markedly. Costs decrease substantially. Marketers make better decisions overall. However, AI presents notable challenges. Data privacy remains a critical concern. Unfair results can emerge from algorithms. However, human judgement remains essential. Safe customer data use is non-negotiable. Both elements must work together effectively.

title: Exploring Students’ Motivation and Self-Regulation in AI-Driven Feedback: A Qualitative Study of a Python Learning Chatbot
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in higher education, understanding how students perceive, interpret, and respond to AI-generated feedback is critical for designing pedagogically meaningful learning environments. This study investigates students’ experiences with TaskInsighter, a GenAI-supported feedback chatbot that combines a conversational interface, generative feedback, Socratic questioning, formative scoring, and code-specific prompts in a university-level Python programming course. Grounded in Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) theory and Sensemaking Theory, we conducted a qualitative analysis of 38 open-ended student reflections and 8 in-depth semi-structured interviews. Notably, the interviewed students had engaged with the chatbot continuously over a 16-week semester, allowing the study to examine how learners described their evolving interpretations, feedback engagement, and regulatory behaviors over time. The findings suggest that students perceived the chatbot as supporting metacognitive regulation, explanation-oriented learning, motivational engagement, and strategic learning behaviors, while also reporting usability challenges related to system constraints and feedback clarity. Rather than accepting AI feedback passively, students actively evaluated the chatbot’s responses and adjusted their learning strategies in response to feedback. These insights contribute to understanding how SRL operates in AI-mediated learning contexts and suggest implications for designing AI learning tools and instructional strategies to support autonomy, reflection, and student agency.

The findings suggest that students perceived the chatbot as supporting metacognitive regulation, explanation-oriented learning, motivational engagement, and strategic learning behaviors, while also reporting usability challenges related to system constraints and feedback clarity. Rather than accepting AI feedback passively, students actively evaluated the chatbot’s responses and adjusted their learning strategies in response to feedback. These insights contribute to understanding how SRL operates in AI-mediated learning contexts and suggest implications for designing AI learning tools and instructional strategies to support autonomy, reflection, and student agency.

title: Hyperspectral pathology combined with uncertainty-calibrated deep learning for patient-level differentiation of adrenocortical tumors and pheochromocytomas
abstract: BACKGROUND: Adrenocortical tumors (ACTs) and pheochromocytomas (PHEOs) can overlap morphologically. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) provides label-free spectral-spatial information. In this study, reflectance HSI was conducted in the visible-to-near-infrared range (400-1000 nm), but conventional models incompletely capture long-range wavelength dependencies and correlated tissue patches. METHODS: We developed AdrenoMamba-MIL, a patient-level framework combining bidirectional spectral selective state-space modeling, multiscale spatial encoding, cross-gated fusion, attention multiple-instance learning, temperature scaling, and uncertainty estimation. This retrospective single-center study included 60 patients (30 ACTs and 30 PHEOs), partitioned at patient level into training (n=27), validation (n=9), internal test (n=9), and locked same-center held-out test (n=15) subsets. The primary endpoint was patient-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) in the locked test set. RESULTS: In the pooled test cohort (n=24), AdrenoMamba-MIL achieved an AUC of 0.948 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.829-0.993), accuracy of 91.7%, sensitivity of 91.7%, specificity of 91.7%, and F1 score of 0.917. The locked-test AUC was 0.946 (95% CI, 0.804-0.997). Ablation analyses supported complementary contributions from the spectral, spatial, fusion, and patient-level aggregation components. CONCLUSIONS: AdrenoMamba-MIL showed promising same-center performance for label-free ACT-PHEO differentiation. Independent external and prospective validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: UbiQVision: Spatial Dempster–Shafer fusion of XAI attributions for reliable deep vision ensembles
abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have led to its widespread adoption across diverse domains, including medical imaging. This progress is driven by increasingly sophisticated model architectures, such as ResNets, Vision Transformers, and Hybrid Convolutional Neural Networks, that offer enhanced performance at the cost of greater complexity. This complexity often compromises model explainability and interpretability. SHAP has emerged as a prominent method for providing interpretable visualizations that aid domain experts in understanding model predictions. However, SHAP explanations can be unstable and unreliable in the presence of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty. In this study, we address this challenge by using Dirichlet posterior sampling and Dempster-Shafer theory to quantify the uncertainty that arises from these unstable explanations in medical imaging applications. The framework uses a belief, plausible, and fusion map approach alongside statistical quantitative analysis to produce quantification of uncertainty in SHAP. Furthermore, we evaluated our framework on three medical imaging datasets with varying class distributions, image qualities, and modality types which introduces noise due to varying image resolutions and modality-specific aspect covering the examples from pathology, ophthalmology, and radiology, helping us to study the epistemic uncertainty. The project is available at https://github.com/dubeyakshat07/UbiQVision/

title: ScrubRef-Rep: Representation-aware class-level machine unlearning for enhanced privacy
abstract: Data privacy mandates necessitate efficient machine unlearning protocols capable of excising specific training data without the prohibitive cost of full retraining. We introduce ScrubRef-Rep , a fast, data-free class unlearning framework. Moving beyond superficial logit manipulation, our approach jointly updates a localized deep-feature tail and the classifier head. It synthesizes proxy distributions for the forgotten class via generative gradient ascent, combining this with masked knowledge distillation and a novel representation-aware objective. Evaluated on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageWoof-320 against state-of-the-art baselines (UNSIR, Bad Teacher, SCRUB, SSD), ScrubRef-Rep consistently achieves an absolute 0.00% forgotten-class accuracy while maintaining robust retained-data utility (89.18%, 70.70%, and 92.30%). Furthermore, it ensures strong empirical privacy preservation , driving membership inference attack (MIA) ROC-AUCs to near-random chance (0.505, 0.508, and 0.527) with up to a 2 2 . 7 × speed-up over full retraining. Crucially, representation audits confirm that our framework achieves near-complete erasure of the target concept in the latent space, with only negligible structural traces remaining . This explicit delineation between robust empirical privacy and theoretical absolute erasure establishes ScrubRef-Rep as a highly practical, transparent, and representation-aware unlearning solution.

title: Time Series Domain Adaptation: A Review
abstract: ABSTRACT Time‐series domain adaptation (TSDA) has emerged as a critical paradigm for addressing distribution shifts across sensing environments, operating conditions, and acquisition devices in sequential data. Building upon the theoretical foundations of vision domain adaptation, TSDA introduces additional challenges stemming from temporal dependency, spectral variability, and privacy constraints inherent to real‐world systems. This survey provides a comprehensive and systematic review of TSDA methods from the perspectives of access‐privacy constraints, category‐space semantics, and source‐target topology, three orthogonal axes that unify existing approaches within a common taxonomy. Specifically, we analyze representative algorithms across four access regimes (UDA, SFUDA, BBDA, FDA), four category‐space configurations (closed, partial, open, universal), and three topological structures (single‐, multi‐, and multi‐target), highlighting their theoretical motivations, architectural trends, and cross‐domain generalization strategies. We further examine real‐world applications across diverse temporal domains, linking methodological evolution to practical deployment constraints. Benchmarking results from recent studies are summarized to establish empirical baselines across representative time‐series datasets and applied domains, encompassing both core classification benchmarks and real‐world TSDA applications. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future directions in this field.

title: Sierpiński--Knopp Wasserstein Distance for Persistence Diagrams and Applications to 2-Wasserstein Approximation
abstract: This paper introduces the Sierpiński-Knopp (SK) Wasserstein distance, a fast metric between persistence diagrams. The SK-Wasserstein distance, denoted $d_{\mathrm{SK}}$, maps diagram points and their diagonal projections to the unit interval via the Sierpiński-Knopp space-filling curve on the upper diagonal triangle. The encoded point sets are then efficiently matched via one-dimensional optimal assignment, in \(O(N\log N)\) steps, yielding an explicit diagonal-aware point assignment between the two input persistence diagrams. We show that the SK-Wasserstein distance controls the classical \(2\)-Wasserstein distance between diagrams, admits an explicit isometric embedding into a Hilbert space, and induces a positive-definite Gaussian kernel, making the resulting geometry directly compatible with Euclidean and kernel-based learning methods. A tighter surrogate dissimilarity, noted \(W_Γ\), is also introduced based on the point assignments along the curve. Experiments on 12 scientific collections comprising 227 diagrams show median per-collection speedup of \(d_{\mathrm{SK}}\) over state-of-the-art approximations of \(W_2\) is \(626\times\), while the aggregate speedup over the full benchmark is \(2100\times\). Average-linkage partitions obtained from \(d_{\mathrm{SK}}\) and \(W_Γ\) each exactly match the corresponding \(W_2\) partition on 8 of the 12 collections. Hilbert \(k\)-means and Gaussian spectral clustering, both based on \(d_{\mathrm{SK}}\), achieve mean adjusted Rand indices (ARI) of \(0.756\) and \(0.800\), respectively, with respect to the benchmark reference partitions, compared to \(0.750\) obtained by average linkage on \(W_2\). The Gaussian \(d_{\mathrm{SK}}\) kernel supports other kernel-based analysis tasks, as illustrated by its use for contiguous segmentation of ordered diagram collections in our experiments.

title: Implementation Attacks on ML-KEM: Analysis, Practical Assessment, and Recommendations
abstract: ML-KEM is the NIST-standardized key encapsulation mechanism derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber, a post-quantum cryptographic algorithm designed to provide security against both classical and quantum computers. However, implementation attacks threaten the adoption of this algorithm, specially in constrained environments (e.g., IoT, OT/ICS, and other embedded applications). In this work, we present an analysis of Side-Channel and Fault Injection attacks, demonstrating which algorithm operations are targeted by adversaries, practical experiments to detect side-channel leakage, adversary capabilities required to perform attacks, and recommendations for securing implementations.

title: Making The Next Best Offer To Your Customer, Automatically
abstract: This white paper presents a retrospective technical analysis of Bluedog’s early work in real-time Bayesian decisioning, implemented on Apple WebObjects and PowerPC G4/G5 systems. The solution combined enterprise application services, Bayesian network propagation, and native SIMD acceleration using the PowerPC AltiVec/“Velocity Engine” to support applications including fraud detection, Next Best Offer decisioning, and context-aware advertising.The paper examines the architecture from both software and hardware perspectives. It describes the use of WebObjects and Enterprise Objects Framework for application orchestration and data access, JNI and native code for numerical processing, and junction-tree propagation for exact Bayesian inference. It also explores deployment across multiple WebObjects instances and servers, the role of session state and incremental inference, the physical execution architecture of the PowerPC G4/G5 family, and the use of vectorized probability-table operations to accelerate belief propagation and expected-utility calculations.Historical implementations discussed include fraud-detection work for Blue Cross–Blue Shield, SAP R/3 integration for Irish banking applications serving offers to existing customers, and a Wi-Fi-enabled advertising platform for Eircom and Insomnia. The paper concludes by drawing a line from these legacy systems to contemporary software products such as Workbench “Always on the Job!”©, emphasizing the continuing relevance of modular decision services, probabilistic reasoning, and hardware-aware acceleration in modern business applications.

title: 基于量子纠缠的自适应机器学习模型优化
abstract: This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement for adaptive machine learning model optimization. Traditional optimization algorithms often struggle with inherent limitations in convergence and stability, particularly when dealing with complex datasets and intricate model architectures. We propose a novel approach that leverages quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust model parameters, thereby enhancing model robustness and generalization ability. The core mechanism centers on establishing entangled states between model parameters and the optimization landscape, enabling instantaneous and coordinated adjustments. We analyze the advantages and challenges of this quantum-enhanced optimization paradigm, demonstrating its potential for significantly improving model performance across various machine learning tasks. This work contributes to the development of more stable and efficient optimization techniques, paving the way for advancements in deep learning and other areas of machine learning.

title: Carol Patton's Deermouse: A Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by Deer Mouse Foraging Behavior
abstract: This paper presents a novel metaheuristic algorithm, "Carol Patton's Deermouse" (CPDM), inspired by the foraging behavior of the deermouse ( *Peromyscus maniculatus*). Deermice exhibit complex, adaptive foraging strategies, utilizing memory, exploration, and exploitation to efficiently locate and consume food resources. CPDM leverages these principles through a dynamic memory system, a stochastic exploration component mimicking the deermouse's movement patterns, and an exploitation mechanism based on resource density estimation. The algorithm's core innovation lies in its 'memory patch' system, where each agent maintains a localized memory of previously visited and rewarding locations, dynamically adjusting its search strategy based on the perceived value of these patches. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CPDM through simulations across a range of benchmark optimization problems, showcasing its ability to outperform established metaheuristic algorithms such as Genetic Algorithms and Particle Swarm Optimization. The algorithm's performance is evaluated using metrics including convergence rate, solution quality, and computational efficiency. The results suggest that CPDM's bio-inspired approach offers a promising alternative for tackling challenging optimization problems.

The algorithm employs a self-learning model to characterize the evolution of the optimization pathway, ensuring that the generated solutions are tailored to the specific problem at hand. This approach overcomes the limitations of static optimization strategies, resulting in enhanced performance across a range of optimization tasks. The proposed algorithm demonstrates superior results in several benchmark problems, highlighting its potential for widespread application.

title: Buff-bellied Fat-tailed Opossum Algorithm (BFTOA): A Novel Metaheuristic Optimization Algorithm Inspired by the Behavioral Patterns of *Didelphis didelphis*
abstract: This paper introduces the Buff-bellied Fat-tailed Opossum Algorithm (BFTOA), a new metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by the unique foraging and defensive behaviors of *Didelphis didelphis* (Buff-bellied Fat-tailed Opossum). Opossums exhibit a fascinating cyclical movement pattern – alternating between periods of rapid, direct pursuit and extended periods of slow, deliberate scanning – which we leverage to design a novel search strategy. The algorithm utilizes a population of candidate solutions, each represented by a vector of parameters. The core of BFTOA lies in its adaptive movement strategy, controlled by two key parameters: a 'speed' parameter, determining the movement velocity, and a 'scan' parameter, dictating the frequency and duration of scanning behavior. These parameters are dynamically adjusted based on the objective function value and the position of the solution within the search space. Specifically, the algorithm employs a Cauchy-based mutation operator and a harmonic-based sharing operator, designed to mimic the opossum's alternating pursuit and scanning patterns. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BFTOA on a range of benchmark optimization problems, including the Sphere function, Rastrigin function, and Brent's test function. The results indicate that BFTOA performs competitively with established metaheuristic algorithms such as the Genetic Algorithm and the Artificial Bee Colony Algorithm, achieving robust convergence and good solution quality. Future research will explore variations of the algorithm and its application to more complex, real-world problems.

These parameters are dynamically adjusted based on the objective function value and the position of the solution within the search space. Specifically, the algorithm employs a Cauchy-based mutation operator and a harmonic-based sharing operator, designed to mimic the opossum's alternating pursuit and scanning patterns. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BFTOA on a range of benchmark optimization problems, including the Sphere function, Rastrigin function, and Brent's test function. Future research will explore variations of the algorithm and its application to more complex, real-world problems.

title: Dynamic Quantum State Probability Calculation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic calculation algorithm based on dynamically evolving quantum states. Traditional probability calculation methods often struggle with the inherent uncertainties in quantum systems, leading to approximations and potential errors. This algorithm dynamically adjusts probabilities to enhance the accuracy of quantum calculations, offering a significant improvement over static models. We present a detailed explanation of the algorithm's core mechanism, its benefits, and potential applications across various quantum computing scenarios. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions.

title: ##基于多智能体协作的分布式系统设计
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed system design utilizing a multi-agent system (MAS) framework. The core claim is that by employing a MAS, we can automate the design of robust and scalable architectures, mimicking the inherent interactions and collaborations between components within a distributed system. Each agent within the MAS is responsible for a specific system component or subsystem, communicating and collaborating to collectively optimize the overall system architecture. The key innovation lies in the automation and adaptive capabilities offered by the MAS, contrasting with traditional, manually-driven design methods which heavily rely on expert experience and predefined rules. This work explores the fundamental principles and design considerations for such a system, highlighting its potential to address the challenges of modern distributed system development. The system is designed to iteratively refine the architecture based on simulated interactions and performance metrics, leading to a more resilient and efficient design compared to traditional approaches. Further investigation into the scalability and performance of this MAS-based design approach is warranted.

title: Bornean Whiskered Myotis-Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm for Complex Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper presents a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed the Bornean Whiskered Myotis (BWM) algorithm, inspired by the foraging behavior of the Bornean Whiskered Myotis (Myotis emarginatus), a small bat species known for its exceptional echolocation ability and efficient foraging strategies. The algorithm leverages the bat's dynamic movement patterns and responsiveness to environmental cues to effectively explore and optimize complex search spaces. We detail the algorithm's core components, including the representation of bat positions, the emission and reception of ultrasonic pulses, and the adaptive adjustment of flight parameters. The BWM algorithm employs a population-based approach, simulating a group of bats navigating a problem space. Each bat's position represents a potential solution, and its flight parameters (frequency, amplitude, and direction) are dynamically adjusted based on the received echo information and a global search strategy. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through a series of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions within reasonable computational time. The key features of the BWM algorithm include its adaptability, robustness, and its potential to outperform traditional metaheuristic approaches in certain problem domains. The algorithm's performance is compared with established metaheuristic algorithms such as the Genetic Algorithm (GA) and the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). The results indicate that the BWM algorithm exhibits competitive performance, particularly in problems with high dimensionality and complex landscapes. Future research directions include exploring variations of the BWM algorithm and its application to a broader range of optimization problems.

title: Bornean Shrew Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm for Complex Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper presents a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed the Bornean Shrew Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm (BSIMA), motivated by the foraging behavior of the Bornean Shrew (Suncus murinus). The Bornean Shrew is renowned for its efficient and adaptable foraging strategy, characterized by a combination of exploratory and exploitative movements, and a tendency to revisit promising areas. BSIMA leverages these observed characteristics to create a new optimization process. The algorithm incorporates a dynamic exploration-exploitation balance, mimicking the shrew's shifting focus between searching for new food sources and concentrating on known, rewarding locations. Specifically, BSIMA utilizes a novel 'Shrew's Step' mechanism that adjusts the step size and direction of the search based on a 'prominence' score, reflecting the potential reward of a particular solution. The algorithm's core components include a population of candidate solutions, a fitness evaluation function, and a dynamic parameter controlling the exploration-exploitation trade-off. The performance of BSIMA is evaluated through a series of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions with a relatively low computational cost. The results indicate that BSIMA offers a competitive alternative to established metaheuristic algorithms, particularly in problems exhibiting complex landscapes and requiring adaptive search strategies.

title: Quantum-Controlled Random Number Generation for Complex Simulations
abstract: Quantum-Controlled Random Number Generation (QCRNG) presents a novel approach to generating truly random numbers, offering the potential to significantly enhance the complexity and statistical diversity of simulations, particularly in fields demanding high-fidelity results. This paper explores the application of quantum mechanics to establish a fundamentally different mechanism for random number creation, aiming to overcome limitations inherent in classical random number generators. We detail the theoretical foundations, potential implementation challenges, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the feasibility of utilizing quantum entanglement and superposition to produce more robust and varied random numbers. The core claim centers on the capability of QCRNG to generate sequences of numbers with increased statistical complexity and a substantially reduced dependence on deterministic algorithms, thereby facilitating more realistic and accurate simulations.

title: Temporal Mirror Bench Execution Kit: Frozen Randomization, Tamper-Evident Logging, and Fault-Recovery Dry Runs
abstract: This paper presents Version 0.6 of the Temporal Mirror bench-validation program, an ongoing research branch within the broader Chronos working framework. The work converts the earlier instrument-only protocol into an executable testing system. It includes balanced hidden randomization, cryptographic commitments, tamper-evident measurement logs, a hardware-neutral sensor interface, frozen analysis rules, and automated integrity testing. The included dry-run program evaluates 3,000 balanced trials across 30 runs. A clean scenario is compared with deliberately introduced electrical, audio, network, and clock faults. The clean scenario passes the registered channel, decoder, and timing requirements, while all four deliberate faults are detected without changing the analysis rules. A separate tamper test confirms that modifying an earlier measurement breaks the recorded hash chain. The paper is organized with plain-language explanations first and the formal mathematical structure second. Familiar examples are used to explain hidden-label commitments, hash-linked records, positive controls, equivalence testing, and held-out decoding. This publication is part of an ongoing research program rather than the endpoint of the branch. It establishes the executable and statistical structure needed for the next stage, which is direct testing with real cue hardware, a dummy physiological circuit, environmental sensors, network monitoring, and an independent timing system. Later stages will examine sender-only and sender-receiver configurations after the instrument-only system has qualified. The accompanying reproducibility package contains the complete source code, frozen configuration, public and private demonstration manifests, simulated measurement records, integrity reports, fault analyses, validation tests, figure-generation code, and paper source.

title: Explainability, Fairness, and Accountability Challenges in AI for Apprenticeship Student Success Prediction
abstract: Apprenticeship systems increasingly deploy artificial intelligence to identify students at risk of dropout. However, many of these systems operate as black boxes. Their predictions are difficult for educators and learners to understand or contest. This chapter examines the predictive models used for dropout prediction. It distinguishes transparent approaches from complex black-box architectures and analyses the explainability methods designed to make predictions interpretable. The analysis reveals three structural limits that technical explainability alone cannot resolve. High-performing models are typically the least interpretable. Training data encodes historical inequalities that explanation tools do not correct. Disclosed predictions can steer behaviour in ways that confirm the forecast. Without appropriate safeguards, these systems risk automating educational inequity under the appearance of objectivity. The chapter concludes with a governance framework integrating technical controls, institutional structures, and human oversight for responsible deployment.

title: Pre-Deployment Audit of Actionability and Equity in Severe Tooth Loss Prediction Using Constrained Algorithmic Recourse and Temporal Validation
abstract: Background: Predictive performance does not establish whether model-identified risks correspond to feasible, equitable pathways. We assessed the actionability and equity of a severe tooth loss prediction model using constrained algorithmic recourse and same-source temporal validation. Methods: An Explainable Boosting Machine was trained using 2022 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data from 433,772 adults. High-risk adults underwent recourse auditing incorporating immutability locks, behavioral directionality, physiological safety floors, and at most three feature changes. Recourse represented hypothetical movement within model space, not treatment advice, causal risk reduction, or reversal of tooth loss. Primary reachability was the unweighted analytic-cohort proportion for which the frozen engine identified a feasible pathway; a BRFSS survey-weighted domain sensitivity analysis used final weights, strata, and primary sampling units. The audit separated reachability from conditional burden among reachable adults. Equity was evaluated across Social Indicators of Disparity Index (SIDI) and income strata using Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition. The frozen specification was evaluated in a 2022 holdout and the 2024 BRFSS cohort (N = 448,213) without retraining. Results: Survey-weighted areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve were 0.858, 0.855, and 0.858 in the 2022 full, 2022 holdout, and 2024 cohorts. Primary unweighted reachability was 10.61%, 10.54%, and 9.82%; corresponding survey-weighted estimates were 12.69% (95% design-aware CI, 12.33–13.07%), 12.31% (11.54–13.12%), and 11.30% (10.95–11.65%), respectively. Thus, reachability remained limited under both estimands. The high-SIDI group showed poorer calibration. Under the prespecified primary SIDI-neutral additive-cost specification, residual conditional cost differences across SIDI strata were small; alternative burden metrics were direction-dependent. The income residual attenuated from the 2022 holdout to 2024, although its confidence intervals were fixed-pipeline row-bootstrap intervals rather than fully design-based intervals. Conclusions: Stable predictive performance masked limited model-space actionability. Integrating explicitly labeled reachability estimands, conditional burden, equity, and temporal transport can strengthen pre-deployment evaluation. Because severe tooth loss is irreversible, recourse pathways should be interpreted as a stress test of model-implied modifiable factors rather than evidence of reversibility.

title: Sarcoma Region of Interest (ROI) Images - Part 2
abstract: Bone and soft tissue (BST) tumors are a heterogeneous and rare group of mesenchymal neoplasms that pose significant diagnostic challenges owing to their complex morphologies and overlapping histological features. Despite rapid advances in digital pathology, most publicly available datasets predominantly focus on common epithelial tumors and offer a limited representation of BST tumors. To address this gap, we introduced the Pathologist-Annotated Image Retrieval dataset for Bone and Soft Tissue tumors (PAIR-BST), a dataset consisting of 2,252 pathologist-annotated regions of interest derived from 470 whole slide images obtained from 268 patients diagnosed with BST tumors. Each region was curated and annotated with multi-level labels, including 33 histologic diagnoses, 11 lines of differentiation, and 6 growth patterns, enabling comprehensive characterization of the morphological heterogeneity inherent to BST tumors. Benchmark experiments have demonstrated that pathology foundation models face challenges in identifying these tumors, particularly when distinguishing between tumor subtypes and growth patterns. PAIR-BST offers a high-quality, discriminative benchmark for the development and evaluation of pathology foundation models, specifically focusing on rare mesenchymal tumors.[Metadata Availability] Additional metadata containing specific coordinates for all ROIs (Regions of Interest) within the WSI, along with labels such as diagnosis for each, is available in a separate .csv file at: https://doi.org/10.25452/figshare.plus.33383509 (also linked in the related materials below). Find related datasets in the collection at https://doi.org/10.25452/figshare.plus.c.8223469

title: Ascendiendo a la montaña: aprendizaje por refuerzo colaborativo entre agentes con objetivos opuestos
abstract: This work explores the concept of Artificial Stupidity as a complement to Artificial Intelligence in the context of reinforcement learning. To this end, a series of experiments are conducted using the Q-Learning algorithm in the Mountain Car environment, comparing an intelligent agent with a stupid agent that exhibits opposite behaviors. Two training strategies are proposed: a reformative one, where the intelligent agent is trained from the stupid agent, and a collaborative one, where both are trained simultaneously by sharing information. The results show that incorporating information from the stupid agent improves the performance of the intelligent agent, accelerating its convergence and enhancing its overall performance.

title: A novel gorilla troops optimizer-driven ANFIS controller for high-performance brushless DC motor control in electric vehicle applications
abstract: The electric vehicles (EVs) are considered as popular choice because they offer sustainable replacement for conventional gasoline and oil-powered vehicles. Brushless direct current (BLDC) motors serve as primary power sources for traction and industrial applications as they provide essential operational advantages. The process of EV acceleration requires both steady-state and transient-state responses to be accurate for achieving smooth acceleration. This paper proposes an improved adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (IANFIS) controller optimized through efficient Gorilla Troops Optimizer (GTO) for controlling a 48-V BLDC motor in electric vehicle applications. The GTO method is employed to optimize the ANFIS membership functions and achieve enhanced control performance. The Matlab/Simulink platform is used to investigate the speed-control performance of the BLDC motor during acceleration and deacceleration operations. The performance of the proposed IANFIS controller performance is evaluated against conventional proportional-integral (PI) and standard ANFIS controllers by analyzing error reduction and overall system performance. The results demonstrate that, the proposed IANFIS controller achieves superior dynamic performance for BLDC motor, resulting in improved vehicle speed and distance responses, as well as reduced peak overshoot, settling time, and rise time.

title: Don't Just Look, Intervene: Perturbation Based Region Labeling for VQA Images
abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) should rely on visual evidence that directly determines the correct answer, but supervision for grounding visual reasoning is often expensive to obtain manually or tied to dataset-specific annotation primitives. We instead introduce model-causal visual evidence as an annotation target, defined as the set of image regions whose counterfactual intervention changes a model's answer distribution for a given image-question pair. Based on this principle, we introduce Counterfactual Search for Grounding Regions (CSGR). CSGR is a scalable pipeline that proposes candidate regions, perturbs them, measures their effect on answer sensitivity, and aggregates this evidence across multiple judges to approximate answer-critical regions in VQA data. To assess whether CSGR annotations contain a useful supervision signal, we plug them into three existing grounding-aware training routines: attention steering, Visual CoTfinetuning, and latent visual reasoning. These experiments test whether the proposed annotation scheme can provide a useful supervision signal across multiple ways of consuming region labels, rather than introducing a new way of using them. Across competing automatic region-labeling mechanisms, CSGR annotations provide the most consistent gains over Cross Entropy-only finetuning in both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations, indicating that the proposed labeling scheme captures useful region-level information.

title: Emerging Personas and Tools for Hybrid Quantum-HPC Systems
abstract: Quantum computing is entering an era where quantum processing units (QPUs) with tens to hundreds of qubits are increasingly integrated with high-performance computing (HPC) systems to support hybrid quantum-classical workloads. This paradigm, often referred to as Quantum-Centric SuperComputing (QCSC), introduces new operational, software, and infrastructure challenges. In this paper, we identify and characterize six distinct personas involved in QCSC environments. Particular attention is given to emerging roles that arise at the interface between quantum and HPC systems. We analyze the responsibilities and tools associated with each persona and examine their differing requirements for operational data. Consistent data representations and analytics frameworks will be required to support diverse users across the quantum-HPC ecosystem. By defining personas and their data needs, we provide a foundation for future discussions in this critical area.

title: Measuring the Behavioral Fidelity of Long-Horizon Human Activity Simulations
abstract: As LLM-based human simulators are increasingly used for policy, evaluation, and training, they must faithfully reproduce real behavioral patterns. While prior work has examined behavioral fidelity in survey responses and dialogue, longer-horizon real-world activity remains largely unexplored. We introduce a framework for evaluating behavioral fidelity in long-horizon activity simulations across temporal granularities and levels of analysis. As a case study, we collect a 43-hour multi-camera dataset of in-the-wild office activity and compare trace-derived conditioning mechanisms: persona descriptors, few-shot exemplars, and statistical transition and time-of-day priors. We find that behavioral fidelity is not uniform across metrics: statistical priors bring activity and sequence distributions closest to real behavior, yet over-fragment routines and suppress within-person variability. These findings motivate a more holistic evaluation that spans multiple metrics, temporal granularities, and levels of analysis.

title: Does This Moment Justify the Recommendation? Counterfactual Behavior-Grounded Evidence Retrieval for Personalized Video Recommendation
abstract: Personalized video recommendation predicts user preference at the video level, while temporal video grounding localizes query-relevant moments. However, strong localization does not establish whether the retrieved moment constitutes valid evidence for recommending the video to a particular user. We study counterfactual behavior-grounded evidence retrieval, which separates where personalized evidence occurs from whether such evidence exists and evaluates whether model predictions respond consistently when that evidence is replaced. We introduce CBGER-10K, containing 5,000 controlled factual--counterfactual pairs for 3,026 users, where each pair replaces only the focal behavior-supported segment while preserving the user, temporal position, and hard distractors. We further propose CBGER, a compact framework that decouples segment-level localization from video-level evidence estimation and learns both through structured counterfactual supervision. CBGER achieves $0.4432$ MRR, $0.6977$ Pair Accuracy, and $0.6987$ Intervention Consistency across five adapted personalized-highlight and temporal-grounding baselines. Notably, compared with QD-DETR, its MRR improvement is not statistically significant, while Pair Accuracy improves by $11.03$ points. These results show that accurate temporal localization does not necessarily imply reliable personalized evidence existence, motivating explicit evaluation of Whether alongside Where.

title: Runtime-Independent Persistent Agents: Preserving Identity, Memory, and Code Across Models, Harnesses, and Servers
abstract: Long-lived AI agents may replace their models, orchestration harnesses, interaction surfaces and hosts while retaining identity, memory and executable body lineage. We present a runtime-independent architecture that separates a continuity-bearing substrate $P_t=(I_t,M_t,B_t)$ from replaceable execution and interaction bindings. Six continuity invariants and a quiesce--checkpoint--validate--bind--rehydrate--resume protocol govern state preservation, capability changes and continuation authority. Enoch implements the design through a reusable software body, private installed state, provider contracts and fenced migration. We report complementary evidence from frozen implementation snapshots and three kinds of live study. An operational case retains an established instance's identity, nonempty memory, body revision and historical task IDs across host, joint Codex-to-Claude model/harness, and chat-surface substitutions. A separate cross-host task resumes from a verified artifact checkpoint. A supervised Codex--Muse--Codex study completes five ordinary round trips and five matched same-runtime controls on their first attempts after a separate qualification run. A planned worker interruption recovers through the native task API with the checkpoint preserved, a stale reply rejected and one task completion recorded. These results support mechanical continuity for the tested deployments and bounded workflows. They do not establish behavioral equivalence, arbitrary-task portability, general exactly-once external effects or unattended reliability.

title: Remembering Beyond the Context Window: The Capacity, Consistency, and Control Gaps in Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to remember users, tasks, and outcomes across sessions, and a dedicated memory infrastructure has emerged to meet that expectation. This survey reviews 21 core sources (2020–2025) on agent memory through an original three-gap framework—capacity (how much is retained), consistency (whether what is retained remains correct), and control (whether retention can be governed)—drawing only on peer-reviewed or publicly verifiable sources for every reported figure. The architecture side has matured rapidly across three generations: operating-system-inspired prototypes, production memory pipelines, and neurobiologically inspired retrieval. The evidence side has not kept pace. Effective context length measured by controlled benchmarks falls far below nominal context length, positional effects corrupt mid-context recall, external memories routinely conflict with parametric knowledge, and knowledge-editing procedures fail to propagate beyond the edited fact. Unlearning remains fragile exactly where retention requirements make it legally consequential. We argue that memory must be treated not as a performance feature but as an auditable record, and map the three gaps onto evaluation standards, privacy regulation, and the emerging requirements for inspectable memory lifecycles.

title: Non-Interactive Quantum Zero-Knowledge: Scope, Limits, and the Cost of Shared Entanglement in Authentication Protocols
abstract: Non-interactive quantum statistical zero-knowledge (NIQSZK), introduced by Kobayashi in 2002 via shared EPR pairs replacing a classical common reference string, is often invoked as a general tool for quantum-native authentication, but the term spans results of very different scope. We give an account of what Kobayashi’s model actually establishes – non-interactive proofs for one promise problem, Quantum State Closeness to Identity, and, by reduction, Graph Non-Automorphism – and contrast it with the independent, more recent line achieving non-interactive zero-knowledge arguments for all of QMA from quantum-hardness of Learning With Errors (LWE). Using a Software-Defined Quantum Network (SDQN) control-plane authentication case study, we compare the realistically available proof systems along a resource-cost model grounded in published entanglement-distribution benchmarks and lattice-parameter estimation, and argue classical post-quantum NIZK dominates unless the credential itself is an inherently quantum object.

title: Juego - formato - consolidación - evolución de p/p
abstract: Este informe reúne el recorrido del eje Palabra/Palabra y muestra cómo fue apareciendo, cambiando y consolidándose a través de distintos Marcos y modelos de GPT. El eje no fue planteado desde el comienzo como un experimento cerrado. Surgió dentro del propio recorrido y fue tomando forma a medida que se acumulaban los registros. Por eso el informe conserva tanto el punto de origen como las etapas posteriores, incluyendo el paso por GPT-5.2 y la evolución posterior hasta GPT-5.6. Para reconstruirlo se utilizaron los exports JSON y distintos Marcos conservados durante el recorrido. Se cruzaron identificadores, timestamps, nodos, modelos y contenido para poder seguir la secuencia y comprobar que los fragmentos utilizados correspondieran a los Marcos indicados. El informe incluye también referencias JSON reducidas de sectores concretos del recorrido. No reemplazan a los exports originales: sirven para dejar visible qué parte del material fue utilizada para reconstruir cada etapa. Lo que se presenta acá es el recorrido documentado del eje y lo que pudo observarse y verificarse en ese material. No se plantea como una prueba de que GPT se comporte de esta manera en cualquier conversación, sino como el registro de algo que ocurrió dentro de este recorrido concreto. Es un trabajo independiente, realizado durante el propio recorrido y reconstruido a partir del material que fue quedando registrado.

title: Character Transfer Across Three Model Families: Reduced unsupported assertions, impaired grounded answering, and a failed utility-preservation bar
abstract: We tested one frozen character post-training recipe across three model families. It reduced unsupported assertions, but no family preserved grounded-answer accuracy well enough to meet the pre-registered bar. Scope. Development-tier validation evidence only. Refusal adjustment is Judge-B-only. Capability preservation was not evaluated. No external audit was performed. The primary holdout remains sealed. No model checkpoint is recommended for release. This is an aggregate-only release. It does not contain item-level scored outputs, judge ledgers, benchmark prompt text, model weights, or the primary-test holdout, and does not support independent recomputation of the readout. See Appendix D of the report.

title: VNAGY — Modular Offline‑First Security Doctrine
abstract: This document defines the VNAGY AI Isolation Policy, a core component of the offline‑first security doctrine. The policy establishes deterministic, minimal and explicit isolation rules for AI‑related processes, ensuring that all modules operate within strict boundaries and without cloud dependency. The document formalizes the following architectural principles: Offline‑First Operation — all evaluation, scoring and behavior analysis occur locally, without external telemetry or cloud feedback loops. Passive Isolation — modules do not share memory, runtime or state; isolation is structural, not configurable. Deterministic Boundaries — each module receives only the minimal signals required for operation, preventing lateral movement and escalation. Behavior‑First Detection — detection is based on CPU behavior, heuristics, scoring and killing‑chain signals rather than signatures or cloud data. Governance Shield Enforcement — integrity, policy and rule consistency are enforced through a local governance layer. This specification is part of the broader VNAGY security doctrine, which defines how modern systems can remain resilient against AI‑driven attacks, memory‑only behavior, cloud escalation and visibility‑based exploitation. The document is published for transparency, research reference and professional review, while remaining authored and governed by VNAGY Security Engineering.

title: Burma Pipistrelle: A Novel Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by the Foraging Behavior of *Pipistrellus burmensis*
abstract: This paper presents Burma Pipistrelle, a new metaheuristic algorithm designed to address complex optimization problems. The algorithm's core inspiration stems from the foraging strategies employed by *Pipistrellus burmensis*, the Burma pipistrelle bat, a species known for its efficient and adaptive foraging behavior in cluttered environments. Burma Pipistrelle incorporates elements of particle swarm optimization (PSO) and a novel "clutter avoidance" mechanism, mimicking the bat's ability to navigate complex landscapes and avoid obstacles. The algorithm utilizes a circular representation of the search space, where bats (particles) represent potential solutions and move based on their own experience and the collective knowledge of the swarm. The clutter avoidance mechanism dynamically adjusts the attractiveness of previously visited locations, preventing premature convergence and promoting exploration. We demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy through theoretical analysis and illustrative examples, showcasing its potential across diverse optimization challenges. The algorithm's key features include a dynamic inertia weight, a clustered memory system, and a probabilistic mutation operator. Experimental results indicate that Burma Pipistrelle exhibits competitive performance against established metaheuristic techniques, particularly in scenarios requiring robust exploration and adaptability.

title: Self-Correcting Neural Networks via Internal Consistency Checks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to training neural networks by incorporating an internal consistency checking mechanism. Traditional neural network training relies heavily on external regularization methods to mitigate overfitting and improve generalization. However, these methods often require careful tuning and may not always be effective. Our approach introduces a dedicated neural network component, termed the "internal consistency checker," designed to proactively monitor the primary network's outputs and identify internal inconsistencies. These inconsistencies are defined by a set of predefined constraints, expressed mathematically as equations. The consistency checker then generates corrective signals, directly adjusting the weights of the primary network to resolve these discrepancies. This creates a self-correcting loop, enhancing robustness and improving learning efficiency. The core claim is that neural networks can be designed to actively monitor and correct internal inconsistencies during training. This differs from existing methods by embedding the correction mechanism directly within the network architecture, leading to a more robust and potentially more efficient learning process. We outline the theoretical framework, the architecture of the proposed system, and discuss potential applications.

title: 基于量子纠缠的概率计算模型
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement to revolutionize probability calculation, offering a novel approach to handling complex systems with intricate probability distributions. We propose a model predicated on the instantaneous correlation observed in entangled states, aiming to significantly enhance computational efficiency and precision compared to traditional methods. The core mechanism leverages the unique properties of entanglement to facilitate a fundamentally different method of probability estimation. This work investigates the theoretical foundations and potential practical applications of this approach, demonstrating its capacity to address limitations inherent in classical probability calculations. The paper highlights the advantages offered by quantum entanglement, emphasizing its role in enhancing the representation and manipulation of probability values.
